explain.say: Sing up a ladder of seven notes. In India you might sing Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni. In Brazil, France or Japan you might sing Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Ti. Different words, same ladder! Look at the board: two ways of naming notes.

explain.say: Fantastic singing! Wow fact: in Indian music, Sa and Pa are fixed, so they are never made sharp or flat, while the other notes can bend. And in China, notes are often written as numbers 1 to 7, called jianpu. Challenge: sing Sa Re Ga Ma Pa and then Do Re Mi Fa Sol. Do they match?

faq.a: Sargam is the Indian way of naming the seven notes: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha and Ni. The name comes from the first four: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma.
asks: What is Sa Re Ga Ma?

faq.q: Where does Do Re Mi come from?
faq.a: About a thousand years ago the Italian monk Guido of Arezzo named notes from the start of each line of a Latin hymn: Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La. Ut later became Do, and Si or Ti was added.
asks: Why is it called Do Re Mi?

faq.q: Is Sa the same as Do?
faq.a: Yes, both are the home note, the first step of the scale. Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni lines up with Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Ti.
asks: Is Pa the same as Sol?

faq.q: Which notes never change in Indian music?
faq.a: Sa and Pa are called achal swaras, fixed notes. They are never made sharp or flat, while Re, Ga, Ma, Dha and Ni can have different versions.
A swara is a musical note in Indian music. There are seven main swaras, and some have higher or lower versions, making twelve in all.

facts: Guido of Arezzo, an Italian monk of the 11th century, gave notes the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la.
In Indian classical music, Sa and Pa are fixed notes that are never altered.
